member and a French Canadian from the province of Quebec it is my duty to rise to a question of privilege in respect of a letter published by the Ottawa Citizen in its issue of February 18. The letter is headed "Shadow of Vichy in Canada," and is addressed to the editor of the Citizen in these words:
Winston Churchill says that the lowest point in the war was when the French folded up. French politicians were responsible. Can it happen in Canada that the representatives of French-Canadian political remote control can cause the same thing here?
Think it over. Vichy is still represented at Ottawa. French Canada controls 65 seats in the House of Commons. There are only 245. 'Nuff said.
James E. Brooks Montreal, February 16, 1942.
This James E. Brooks is the president of the James E. Brooks Cotton company, of Montreal. His business address is 614 St. James street, Montreal; his home address is Sea Island Beach, Georgia. The records of the customs offices will show that he deals in cotton imported from United States and Brazilian firms which are enemy controlled.
Does he not know the names Esteve Brothers, or J. Kahn and Company, of Campanera? The money he pays for this cotton goes to Italy or Germany, because it is cotton that was originally bought for and on account of German and Italian principals. He gets it cheap and sells it to well-known Canadian textile firms, who are not averse to exploiting their French-Canadian employees.
The proof of this could be found in the files of the customs department. If a return were tabled of Canadian firms which trade with the enemy, no French-Canadian firm would be found in that list; only good "patriots" who are shouting for conscription. And no French Canadian is on the board of directors of any such company.

maintopic: SUSPENSION OP STANDING ORDER 21 TO PROCEED WITH BILL THIS DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in announcing on Friday evening the business for to-day, I did not mention the possibility of the house considering the plebiscite bill. I did refer to the matter on the previous evening. I then stated that if the bill were given its second reading that evening it was possible that we might be in a position to consider it on Monday when it would have been reported back to committee of the whole.
The bill has just been reported back to committee of the whole and, as the leader of the opposition and all hon. members are aware, the government is anxious to proceed with it as quickly as possible. Under the circumstances I was going to ask if hon. members would give their consent to proceeding with discussion of the bill in committee of the whole to-day. If we are to proceed a motion will, of course, be required, because the rule is that there must be forty-eight hours' notice after a bill is reported back from any standing or special committee before it can be considered. There is another rule, however, which provides that in respect of an important matter consent may be obtained and a measure proceeded with.
If the house would give its consent I should like to move:
That bill No. 10, an act respecting the taking of a plebiscite in every electoral district in Canada and the taking of the votes at such plebiscite of Canadian service voters stationed within and without Canada, be considered in committee of the whole this day and that standing order 21 be suspended in relation thereto.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS MADE BY ORDER IN COUNCIL UNDER WAR MEASURES ACT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: AMENDMENTS MADE BY ORDER IN COUNCIL UNDER WAR MEASURES ACT
speechtext:
I have frequently had occasion to call the attention of the government to the fact that while parliament was in session orders in council have been passed changing the statute laws of this country but I have never had an instance that was so coincident in point of time as the one to which I now desire to call attention, namely, the order in council P.C. 1372 passed on February 23, 1942. This order in council was passed under the War Measures Act and suspends the operation of subsection 4 of section 11A of the Precious Metals Marking Act for the duration of the war and six months thereafter.
Labour Conditions

Hon. members will recall that on the very day this order in council was passed under the War Measures Act this house gave second reading to a bill to amend the Precious Metals Marking Act, considered it in committee and then gave it third reading, and we were never told for a moment that a very much more important change in the law was being made under the authority of the War Measures Act by order in council.
I should like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce why as a matter of principle the government did not in these circumstances seek to suspend section 11A by act of parliament, which could have been passed! on February 23, rather than by order in council passed on that day. The provisions of section 11A, suspended, were not important, but they are very much more important than the provisions of the bill which will shortly become an act of parliament. I think this is treating parliament with contempt.

It is impossible to state how many factories producing war supplies are working full time and how many are working only part time. Many plants producing war supplies have only a portion of their employees so engaged. The rest of their employees are working on civilian production.

Plebiscite Act

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE

speechtext:
Hon. N. A. McLARTY (Secretary of State) moved that the house go into committee on Bill No. 10, respecting the taking of a plebiscite in every electoral district in Canada and the taking of the votes at such plebiscite of Canadian service voters stationed within and without Canada.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Fournier (Hull) in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
I think it might be appropriate, before we proceed too rapidly with the bill, that I should make a few observations in connection with the work of the special committee that was appointed to consider it. I do not think it necessary to make them at any length.
In the first place the committee met and gave intensive study to the measure, even though in point of days consumed the time was short. It will, I think, be a matter of gratification that the report is unanimous, that all shades of opinion were able to agree on the particular enactment that the committee had to consider.
The committee not only considered the particular clauses of the bill, but as the bill provides and as was announced at the time the motion was introduced and upon second reading, regulations to implement the provisions of the bill were also considered.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext: Will they be before this committee?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
I would say not. I think any matter relating to them, any question as to procedure, questions as to scrutineers and things of the kind might properly receive the attention of this committee, but the regulations are not part of the bill. Three provisions were applied, however, which should make the regulations fair in their application.
First, it is provided in the bill itself that these regulations shall as far as possible comply with the sections of the Dominion Elections Act. That would apply largely to the case of the ordinary voter. In the case of the service voter, however, the regulations, which are under separate cover and form a section by themselves, comply with the regulations that were used in the last dominion election in 1940 to take the vote of service voters.
A third point which I might suggest is that while it is undoubtedly undesirable to impose penalties by way of regulations, no penalty is provided under the existing regulations which the committee approved, so far as it
had any authority to approve them, that is not contained in the Dominion Elections Act, save one. That is the provision of the bill as to vouching and illegal voting by way of the vouching provisions, so that every penalty clause included in the regulations has received the consideration of the parliament of Canada. In other words the specific regulations relating to ordinary voters are an adaptation as closely as possible of the provisions of the Dominion Elections Act. So far ns they relate to service voters they are an adaptation of the regulations used in the last dominion election, which apparently worked successfully. I believe the regulations have been distributed to hon. members, as was the bill, after consideration by the special committee. Consequently, I suggest that there can be no possible objection to giving to the committee any information that may be required as to specific points covered by the regulations, but to go over the regulations clause by clause as we undoubtedly shall on the bill, in the case of both ordinary voters and service voters, would probably be an undue waste of time of this committee and of the house.
With these few general remarks I should like to deal with the amendments, because the committee did make some amendments to the bill. The principle of the bill has been debated at length, but despite that fact the special committee gave careful and considered attention to the respective sections. In general, it may be said three principal amendments have been made. The first of these is to ensure that the bill is not general, but specific in application. That is done by a definite amendment to section 3 by setting out therein the form and terms of the ballot, and by making other necessary minor changes, such as changing "a" to "the" when it is necessary to prescribe a particular limitation in respect of the plebiscite. That is the first important amendment.
The second amendment extends the coverage of the bill to include a situation which arose in connection with the Yellowknife administration district. The bill itself refers to electoral districts. This was a district which had grown up within the last few years, but which was not included within the definition of the term "electoral district". Representations were made by representatives of the council of the northwest territories to the effect that the people who had settled in the Yellowknife administration district within the last few years should not be disfranchised. The committee saw fit to accede to the representations thus made, by adding a new paragraph (d), the wording of which includes the administration district of Yellowknife.
Plebiscite Act

This is a compact district, having something like 1,400 voters all within a radius of three and a half miles. Although it is a new district, the act of disfranchising them appeared to the special committee both unjustified and unjustifiable.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
Are they
at present in any electoral district?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
No, they are not, and
that is why we have had to have a specific paragraph (d); otherwise they would not be included. It is true that there are others in the northwest territories who might have been considered, but it was thought to be impracticable to include them because of the vast area and the tremendous expense which might be involved. The committee sought to extend the bill as far as possible without involving any great measure of expense in connection with the vote.
The third major amendment is that found in paragraph (c) of subsection 2, section 4. During his observations the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) pointed out that in that paragraph we were leaving with the provinces the possibility of regulating as to those who might vote in the plebiscite. It is remarkable, I believe, that in the plebiscite of 1898 provincial lists were used exclusively.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext: We had no federal lists then.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
No, as the leader of the opposition has said, we had no dominion lists. Prohibitions were made in the elections act of 1938; but in order that there might be no misapprehensions in the matter we have provided in paragraph (c) that the provincial enactment shall be operative only at the time of the coming into force of this act. It precludes any possibility, as suggested by the hon. member for Rosthern, that between now and the taking of the plebiscite provincial legislation could be extended to disfrancise other voters in Canada.
I believe those are the main amendments recommended by the special committee. A perusal of the bill will indicate the minor changes. I might explain that the words inserted in paragraph (c) of subsection 2, section 4, are "at the time of the coming into force of this act." The leader of the opposition will recognize the change. It merely limits any change in the provincial right to amend an election list to the time when the act comes into force.
I believe I have dealt with all the important amendments. Minor changes must necessarily be made in order to give effect to the chief amendments. Then, some other matters were considered by the special committee. In the debate on the resolution and

These special returning officers will distribute ballot papers, envelopes and other plebiscite supplies to commanding officers named by the Department of National Defence and stationed in the territory under their jurisdiction. Such commanding oificers will designate a commissioned officer attached to his unit to take the votes of the members of such unit. As at the last dominion election, what is termed postal voting will be resorted to in the recording of such votes. The voting will be held on nine week days immediately preceding polling day. The hours of voting will be fixed by the commanding officer, but shall be not less than three each day.
When a Canadian service voter seeks to vote at the polling place, he will first be required to complete a declaration giving his full name, his regimental number, that he is a British subject, that he has not voted before at the plebiscite, that he ordinarily resided in Canada prior to his enlistment, and giving the name of the place, with street address, of such ordinary residence in Canada.
When this declaration has been duly completed and signed by both the voter and the commissioned officer, the voter will be handed a ballot paper in practically the same form as that used in Canada, and an inner envelope, and will go to a compartment and there secretly mark his ballot paper. The ballot paper will then be folded, and, in full view of the commissioned officer, placed in the inner envelope. The inner envelope will then be placed into an outer envelope addressed to the special returning officer, and upon which the postage is paid. The voter will then himself mail the envelope at the nearest post office or mail box.
Upon receipt of the outer envelopes in the office of the special returning officer, they will be examined and parcelled in lots of 500. Each parcel being labelled with a consecutive number and stored in a safe place until the counting of the vote begins.
At six o'clock on polling day the special returning officer and his staff will count the ballot papers included in each lot of 500 and

a special statement of the count will be completed in the ease of each lot. A period of one week is allowed for the counting of the votes of Canadian service voters.

As soon as this is done, the special returning officer will transmit to the chief plebiscite officer a statement giving the number of votes cast in the affirmative and in the negative, respectively, in each of the lots of 500 outer envelopes parcelled as above referred to.

Mr. Chairman, as I said a moment ago, it is my intention now to read a very important and magnificent letter which has been sent by a great Canadian citizen to the Prime Minister of Great Britain. It was received by Mr. Churchill this morning, having been sent across via ferryscommand. The letter is dated Montreal, February 25, 1942, and reads:
The Right Honourable
Winston Spencer Churchill,
Prime Minister,
10 Downing Street, London, England.
Mr. Prime Minister:
A citizen of the commonwealth, no matter how humble, always enjoys the right to communicate with the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, to give him his reflections and make known to him his thoughts. There are moments, rare it is true, when the right becomes a duty. I think that, for the writer, that moment has arrived, sir.
Mr. Prime Minister, the citizen who writes is a Canadian of the French language, a loyal subject of the King of Canada, faithful to the culture of his forebears, devoted to the Franeo-British union in Canada, who prays with all his power for a total war effort. He believes that the future of the world rests in the victory of the united nations and their defence of free institutions.
He is one of your admirers, for you are the great heroic figure of the war. Victorious over the treachery of the appeasers you have, in an
Plebiscite Act

hour of tragic responsibility become the spirit incarnate of British resistance, the spirit of the Commonwealth's sacrifice, the spirit of victory itself. With that spirit you have inspired the whole coalition. After the abandonment of Czechoslovakia, stupid and dishonourable as it was; after the destruction of Poland; after the disaster of Norway; after the defeat of Holland and Belgium; after the fall of France; Britain stood alone with the commonwealth nations against the nazi monster. The position of Russia was uncertain and ambiguous; the United States, far away in distance and in its own state of mind, disarmed, its people devoted to the ways of peace, believed itself safe behind the two oceans which lave its shores. In this desperate plight you alone were not desperate, did not despair. You communicated your hope and courage to all men. Led by you, Britain faced with high hope whatever sacrifice might be met, faced it alone with her sister nations of the commonwealth, engaging her very existence and that of her empire. Because your magnificent words have spurred men to new hope, because Britain made it known that she would perish before she would yield, you have brought home to men everywhere the prime condition of victory . . . the will to win.
To-day you are faced by a new task, one more difficult and which will call for the exercise of new virtues in you. Victory will not adorn your standards until you accept the new task with all the tenacity which marks your very appearance. You have united the will and the conscience of all men of good will to fight for freedom, have done it with brave heart and brave words. Now we must go on and win.
Now we must win . . . It is no longer a question of eloquence.
Now it is a question of eternal vigilance, of intelligent imagination, of sternness in criticism, of passionate devotion of the services, who certainly yearn for victory but which, in all truth, are overburdened by a stiff-necked bureaucracy at the top. The duty of our political leaders is undoubtedly to protect the fair name of the services, if only for the sake of the dignity of the homeland, and there are times when, for this very reason, the statesman must suffer attack in silence. But the duty of the political leader is. above all, to control, to criticize, to inspire, to discipline the services of the state, both civil and military, to eliminate from them all uselessness and paralysis and to imbue them with fighting spirit, imagination, realism and the will to action. Never believe, sir, that the services will reform themselves from within; every biological organism, or social organism, always attempts by natural law to retain its existing form and being. It is only possible to change it from without. We cannot change the natures of men. But we can change men.
I do not think, Mr. Prime Minister, that I am unduly pessimistic. I believe with all my heart in the possibility, the hope, of victory. But we shall have to. change methods and we shall have to change men. The democracies always seem to believe that it is sufficient to change ministers. That is only a beginning. Changes are urgently needed, at the top, in all the services of the state. Unless the series of disastrous events is to continue we must find men of initiative to undertake command of our forces, our technical departments and the

services of the state as a whole. The cry of the ostrich: "The British only win one battle in any war; the last one!" still seems to be our slogan. The Lords of the Admiralty still think, no doubt, that it is enough to be British to be invincible and to them the column which commemorates Trafalgar and the spirit of Nelson in itself constitutes a definite promise of victory. Was it not Kipling who said: "If blood be the price of Admiralty, Lord God we have paid in full!"?
I do not wish to make a dolorous inventory of the series of disasters which have attended us on the seas. They provide a stern indictment against Britain's senior services. These continuous disasters have seriously impaired the spirit of all men, sir. Bring into your mind's eye, before your coldest and most lucid judgment, the effects of just the most recent on even the most resolute hearts .	.	. The
Prince of Wales and the Repulse, redoubtable and magnificent instruments of naval science, yet sent to the bottom almost instantly, for lack of aerial defence.	Think of the
Scharnhorst, Gneisenau and Prim Eugen, bombarded for months in the harbour of Brest, yet with an insolent defiance which commands respect, braving Britain's power as they forced the Channel and the straits of Dover, despite the Royal Navy, the Royal Air Force and the guns of Dover.
What food for thought such occasions create! Do not tell us, as the services would like us to believe, that the escape of these three ships from Brest is a victory, or at least an amelioration of sea-problems, almost as though the great ships of the Royal Navy had let them through the Straits for that reason. You have courageously offered the people blood, sweat and tears. They accept this new defeat with grim resolution. They will accept more. But your duty and your policy must be to limit to the smallest inevitable amount this expenditure of blood, sweat and tears of a determined people.
It is no longer a question of heart or of eloquence. To-day the problem is one for the intelligence, one of implacable reform in high places. It is not possible for men to work 24 hours a day. But the departments of war must work without respite and with true intelligence if we are to win. Rejuvenate your Admiralty, sir. Do not judge all men by yourself, Mr. Prime Minister; not all the old men enjoy your physical and mental youth. Cut down by ten and twenty years the ages of all the men at the top. Forget peace-time rules of advancement. Let the young generals who win successes on the field receive without delay, not medals, but immediate increase in the importance of their commands. Surround yourself with twenty or a hundred young men . . . military men, naval men, aviators, men of science, engineers, business men . . . whose function it will be to think, and plan. Let it be their mission to exercise a passionate, endless, zealous watch over all the services of the state, military, naval, air force, foreign affairs, whatever these may be. Inspire these young men with your own spirit, as young men in other countries have been inspired to leadership by another passion, the nazi doctrine.
Our combatants are pledged resolutely to the supreme sacrifice. Our material of war reaches immense proportions and it grows from day to day with prodigious speed. With such great

Plebiscite Act
resources at your command, in men and munitions, do not permit the victory of our cause to be delayed forever by the ingrained bureaucracy of old men of old mind.
We cannot lose the war. You have said so with moving eloquence which has stirred the whole world, rekindling its hope and its determination. But, Mr. Prime Minister, I put it to you that we cannot make the right moves on the chessboard of war if we leave the responsibility for decision to fossilized old men in uniforms.
Think, as often men did during the course of the last war, of the magnificent statue of the Victory of Samothrace, which was intended to crown the prow of a victorious battleship. It was clad in the wind. Its wings were spread for flight. But the Victory had no head! We cannot fight in such terms to-day. The true direction of this war depends upon creative minds, on organization, on skilled and determined leadership. What we need is not committees of old men in uniforms who come together occasionally to discuss the problems of the war as a matter of course, or- duty, but who leave all initiative to the enemy. We need a brain trust, young and energetic, of whom constructive thinking, imagination, determination and daring will be expected daily . . . men who are not afraid to act, men who are not still fighting the last war . . . men who will brush aside all obstacles, permanent officials of alert and innovating mind. This is the urgent need in the armed forces and in all branches of administration of the war.
This is the price of victory.
Mr. Churchill, your back is against the wall, face to face with this task. Discharge it well and men will follow you to the ends of the earth.
I have the honour to be,
Mr. Prime Minister, Respectfully yours,
Emile Vaillancourt.

Whatever observations I have to make to-day will be confined to the bill immediately before us. I regret to have observed, as the ' minister proceeded, that certain recommendations which I made-I believe it was in the committee stage on the resolution-have been rejected by the committee. I shall deal with these briefly as I come to them, but I want to register immediately a vigorous protest against the statement made by the minister near the conclusion of his remarks, that the service votes are to be counted en masse. I think the soldiers, sailors and airmen will want it to be known how they voted in relation to their constituencies, and, if that is not possible, at least in relation to their provinces. To allocate the votes in the general amount as pro and con will not, I think, be satisfactory to the men themsleves, and certainly it will not be satisfactory to us.
The bill which is now before the committee, the reprint as a result of the committee's report, differs entirely in principle, although not in form, with certain exceptions, from the bill to which second reading was given last week. I think it is the most awkward kind of drafting I have ever seen, to take a general bill of this kind and superimpose limitations upon it and make it a special bill applicable to one particular situation. From the standpoint of draftsmanship it could not be worse. I do not know why the bill was ever introduced in the form in which it was brought down unless it was the policy of the government to have the principle of the plebiscite in our system. I do not think for a moment that that was ever the intention of the Prime Minister. Certainly there was no utterance of his or of the Secretary of State which would give justification for that principle. The bill should have been withdrawn and brought down as a special bill designed to take this plebiscite. Instead of that, we have superimposed on the bill special limitations, including the ballot itself, as promised by the Prime Minister; but the rest of the bill is general in its character.
I do not suppose the government will at this late stage accept the suggestion which I made last week and withdraw the bill and bring it back in the form which good draftsmanship would dictate. With the limitations imposed by the amendments, that is to say, the limitation with respect to the ballot, and with the limitation that the ballot shall only be applicable to this plebiscite and no other plebiscite, I am in agreement. This parliament has not passed on those regulations. For a government to bring down a measure imposing penalties by regulation which might land a man in gaol without the people's representatives having anything to say about the matter savours at least of dictatorship, if nothing worse. I do object to that. In a democratic country to impose penalties involving the liberty of the subject without the [DOT]people's representatives having anything to say is an absolute negation of liberalism, of democracy.
I do not want to discuss the penalties. The minister has said that the regulations follow, as nearly as may be, those in the elections act. I would point out one exception. In this country we have been against the idea of the numbered ballot, because without doubt it is a method whereby the secrecy of the ballot is destroyed. If the minister will turn to section 28 of the Dominion Elections Act, chapter 46 of 1938, subsection 5 reads:
(5) The ballot papers shall be numbered on the back of the stub and the counterfoil, the same number being printed or written on the stub as on the counterfoil; each ballot paper shall bear on the back thereof an impression of the stereotype block supplied by the chief. electoral officer pursuant .to subsection 2 of section 13 of this act.

Plebiscite Act
Then it goes on to say that the ballot paper shall be bound up. Section 15 of the ordinary voter plebiscite regulations reads:
15. (1) Immediately after the issue of the proclamation, the chief plebiscite officer shall cause the ballot papers to be used at the plebiscite held under the Dominion Plebiscite Act, 1942, and these regulations, to be printed on both sides, consecutively numbered, perforated and bound in books of twenty-five. . . .
If that clause is left in the regulations, every deputy returning officer and any man in the voting booth will be enabled, if he so desires, to leant how every voter voted. I do not think the minister intended that. I do not understand how that escaped the eagle eyes of the members of this committee, unless they are going to adopt a new principle and hereafter we are going to have numbered ballots. If that is going to be the case in Canada, look out. I do not know any better chance for tracing a voter's ballot and finding out how he voted. The numbered counterfoil I understand. That is a safeguard against fraud from the time the ballot leaves the hands of the deputy returning officer and is taken into the secret compartment until it is brought back and delivered to him. That is quite proper. But that is detached before the ballot is deposited in the box. I hope the Prime Minister, who is following me closely, will get my point. To have the ballot numbered as provided by clause 15 of these regulations is to provide a method whereby the secrecy of the ballot is destroyed. I ask hon. members to study this thing and test it. I ask that that regulation be changed, and I do not think I ought to have to elaborate the reasons why. There is no doubt that this is not in conformity with the elections act. I have demonstrated that. It is not a real adaptation of subsection 5 of section 28 of the act to which I have referred. If this is kept in the regulations, it is a violation of every principle of the secrecy of the ballot, enabling identification of voters, and it opens the door to abuses of the most glaring kind. I appeal to the government to have that changed. A very simple wording in the regulations following the provisions of subsection 5 of section 28 of the act will bring about the cure I am seeking. I think I should not have to argue that any further. Everybody will agree that we ought to preserve the secrecy of the ballot. I do not understand how the chief electoral officer, having regard to the provisions of subsection 5 of section 28, ever put that in the regulations, or what he had in mind. Certainly I would not for a moment think the government instructed him to do it.

Unless these regulations have been checked with the greatest care, there may be other instances where there has not been a proper adaptation of the provisions of the elections act. I pointed out to the house in the committee stage that the regulations should be instructive and interpretative, but that they should not be enacting or legislating.
That is a very sound principle, but it has not been followed. Apparently it never was the intention of the government to follow it. I admit it would take time but, after all, this is an important matter, even though it is now limited to one plebiscite. We ought not to do by regulation that which heretofore and under the general law of the country is done by legislative enactment. There is no doubt in the world about the power of the government to change any of these regulations. Just let us look at section 9:
9. (1) The governor in council may, for the purposes of this act, make such regulations as are expedient for the effectual taking of the plebiscite and, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, for the printing, distribution and publication of the act and instructions issued thereunder, the preparation of voters' lists and other documents.
I refer particularly to subsection 3:
(3) Any regulations made under this act shall have the same force and effect as if enacted in this act.
I protest against legislation by regulation, even though the necessity for speed, from the government's point of view exists. This is wrong in principle, and it ought not to be followed in practice. I can just hear the welkins ring if my right hon. friend were in my place, and I were over there! He would object to this-make no mistake about it- and he would be right. I have thrown out in a gentlemanly manner the suggestion that the government ought not to do this sort of thing. My suggestion has been entirely ignored. This is not right; it is not good legislation, and it is not democracy.
In the course of my previous observations I made reference to the production of registration certificates. The committee did me the honoui of investigating the matter but, according to the Secretary of State they were unanimous against my suggestion. I tell the minister and the committee that there are a large number of people in Canada who never registered under the national registration scheme. How great that number is I do not know. But I would
Plebiscite Act

point out the law of the country states that everybody shall carry his registration certificate. Those people who did no.t register are shirkers, and ought not to be allowed to vote in a plebiscite which may, or may not, mean a great deal.
Any man who has not registered should not be permitted to vote. Every good citizen will have his registration certificate. I have carried mine, although I have never been asked to show it. I am sure, however, that each hon. member carries his registration certificate. The present bill allows a man who never intended to register, a man who may be a shirker, and everything else, to exercise his franchise. Is that a proper principle to encourage? The carrying of a registration certificate is no hardship. The Secretary of State has said it was the opinion of the committee that some people from rural areas might have forgotten their registration certificates. I heard about a man who died, and in whose safety deposit vault was found his registration certificate. That is the last place I should think it ought to have been. I know of no place where a man could get it less quickly.
There is no real reason in the world why a man should not produce his registration certificate, if he wishes to vote. This is a time of war, and it was my understanding that national registration was primarily intended to line up the man-power and woman-power of a nation. There have been cases of prosecutions for non-registration; there have been other cases of prosecutions for fraudulent connection with registration, and there have been other prosecutions with respect to the issuing of floating registration certificates. I cannot, however, conceive of any good reason why the government should give a vote to the man who for safety's sake, shall I say, did not register. I suppose it is now too late to make the necessary change. I would point out, however, that it is the law of the country that every man shall carry his registration certificate. If the government does not place in these regulations or in the bill something such as I have suggested, it will be saying in effect to'the man who did not register, "Well, it is the law of the country, but we are not going to enforce that law."
May I now turn to the question of the open vote in urban municipalities. I said on an earlier occasion that open voting in rural districts, where a man could be vouched for by another elector, was a safe and proper procedure, because everybody knows everybody else. There would always be someone who could properly vouch for a prospective voter, and subscribe to the terms of the oath. But I tell the Secretary of State that in large urban centres the open vote will be subject to rMr. R. B. Hanson.]
great abuse; it will be an instrument of fraud. Why, there is not anything in certain constituencies of the city of Montreal which is not resorted to at election time. It is well known that elections in Montreal are-I cannot summon language adequate to describe the fraud practised. They had nothing in Tammany Hall on election methods in Montreal.
I have heard of cases in smaller areas, under
10.000	persons where one man vouched for dozens of electors. My colleague will speak about that, later in the debate. You see, it becomes a racket, and I say this practice of open voting ought not to apply to the big urban centres. I have had no experience in other large urban areas, such as Toronto, but I have heard stories about what obtained at some points, and my information leads me firmly to the conviction that we cannot be too careful m our provisions to ensure honest voting in some of the big cities. There are all kinds of frauds. This measure lends itself to that type of fraud, when nobody knows anybody else, and it will become a racket. I suggest to the Secretary of State that the fact that certain members feel that the system of open voting has worked well in certain rural areas is no argument with respect to urban areas, because conditions are entirely different. The premise upon which one reaches the conclusion that a system may work well in one given situation, does not exist in the other situation.

As a rule, these men are concentrated fairly well, although there may be a few isolated cases. I am thinking of the men overseas who are all in Great Britain. But what about Canadians who are operating with the Royal Air Force? What about the several hundred Canadians who are with the Royal Navy? These boys would like to vote. are going to be made to take care of these boys? As I said, there are a great many Canadians in the Royal Canadian Air Force who are operating with the Royal Air Force, and they are not segregated by any means. 1 saw them working under Royal Air Force direction in certain parts of the old country. Are they to have a chance to vote? I am afraid, unless we get some assurance, they will not be given a chance to vote.
I do not see much difficulty about the army except where they may be isolated. I understand there are Canadian engineers in Gibraltar, and there may be some Canadians acting as observers in Libya and that sort of thing. I would think it would be almost an impossibility to get their votes, but what about the men at Gibraltar? I think it is most important that every service vote should be polled at this plebiscite. Certainly these men will have opinions on this question, and they are at a disadvantage as compared with the men at home. The greatest care will have to be exercised to get the service vote out.
I regret I have not had1 time to do more than read the memorandum which the minister quoted this afternoon and which outlines what is proposed to be done. I have not had time to read the regulations under which the service vote is to be taken. I should like to point out to the minister that in the last election a substantial proportion of the service votes was not polled. I have not a memorandum in front of me from which I could give the exact figure, but no doubt the authorities will know just what proportion was not polled. There was a substantial proportion polled in Canada, but in England all the service vote was not polled.
To sum up briefly, because I do not want to keep the committee too long, I object to the draftsmanship of the bill, but I am bound to admit as a lawyer that, awkward as it may be, it meets the objection which I have. This bill will die in law at the conclusion of the plebiscite. It is fairly good draftsmanship with respect to the general bill, but when you have superimposed these limitations and restrictions, from the point of view of legal draftsmanship it is just a botch. I still think the suggestion I made as to the production of registration certificates is sound for the reasons I gave. No man who has not registered should be allowed to vote in this or any other election.
I am going to deal with certain sections in the bill when we reach them, and I shall ask the minister for definite information. He has announced an amendment to section 4 which deals with the disqualification of voters to make this relate to the time of the coming
into force of the measure. This will be quite definite if the principle involved in this section is adhered to. I assume that that will be the case and this, of course, remedies certain objections which were raised in the committee. I shall ask the minister certain questions about this matter of disqualification.
I intend to refer particularly to the Douk-hobors. When we were in the west we saw some of these gentry, and we were told that the women worked the farms while the men hired out. The young men did not register under the mobilization act, and they were waiting around to take the jobs of other young men who enlisted in the active service forces. As labour gets scarcer, no doubt many of these Doukhobors will be able to get positions. I do not think that is a situation which ought to obtain in Canada. I do not know just what the provincial law is in British Columbia, but perhaps the minister will be prepared to give us details of the provincial laws that bar certain people from voting. We shall want to know about the Japanese and how many soldier Japanese will be permitted to vote. There will be other questions of a similar nature.
I mentioned the Doukhobors. A young man who comes forward to vote, certain other conditions prevailing, will lose his right to postponement of military service. Therefore he is not apt to come forward to vote. What about his father andi mother, his cousins, his sisters and his aunts? Are they to be allowed to vote in Saskatchewan, we shall say? I raise the question and* I want some information. A young man will not fight; he will not come forward to register, but his whole family will vote. I know it is a difficult matter to deal with, but this has been the position ever since these people came here. Then there are the Mennonites. Personally I do not know much about them.
I read with a great deal of interest the orders in council which relate to these conscientious objectors. I must say that the legal interpretation which I put upon these is not the same as has been put upon them heretofore by both parties, but it may be that that has been done for the purpose of avoiding trouble. You can lead a horse to water, but you cannot make him drink. There is a good, deal of truth in that old saying. You can say that a man must work, but it is pretty hard to make him work. There is the celebrated case in the English law reports dealing with the opera singer, about which the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) spoke. \ ou can restrain her from singing for somebody else, but you just cannot make her sing for you. There are physical

limitations about these things, and it may be that the interpretation that has been given in days gone by to some of these orders in council with respect to conscientious objectors has been given for the purpose of saving trouble to those in authority. I am not urging anything; I am just looking for information. If we have to have this plebiscite bill, let us have it and get it over with and get on with the war.

Mr. Chairman, in rising
to speak on this plebiscite bill at this stage I find myself still tremendously confused as to why we are now facing the responsibility of passing such a bill as this seems to be. I am still confused over whether the people realize what they are voting for. I have tried to think my way through it. I have read many statements that have been made, particularly by the Prime Minister; I have studied not only the statements he made in the past few days but statements he made some lime ago, and I am still confused. Perhaps I am not very brilliant, but I maintain that if I am confused over the issue, there are a lot of other people in Canada who are confused over it too.
I recall that last fall the Prime Minister, speaking on the issue of military service for overseas, made this statement in the house on November 12, 1941, rising to a question of privilege. I believe the press at that tune were pressing him in respect to an all-out war effort, and as reported at page 4321 of Hansard of November 12, 1941, the Prime Minister used these words:
I want it to be distinctly understood that so far as the principle of compulsory selective national service is concerned for Canada, m Canada, I stand for that principle. I have never taken any other stand. It is the position that I have held all along. It has been applied in connection with military training and applied in a number of other directions 1 might mention. How much further it will be applied the house will learn as the government takes its decisions on that matter.
But so far as conscription for service overseas is concerned in the armed forces of Canada, that question was submitted to the people of Canada at the last general election, an election which was held in war time, and in which the leaders of nil political parties made their statements to the electorate, and the people of Canada decided against conscription for overseas service. So far as I am concerned, without any consultation of the people on that subject, I do not intend to take the responsibility of supporting any policy of conscription for service overseas.
That is a clear and definite statement. I have nothing to say against it. It is bold; it is open; it cannot be misunderstood.
The question that is confusing me to-day is whether the people of Canada are now to be asked to vote on that issue which the Prime

Minister said he would submit to the country. The reason why I am confused is this, that when the Prime Minister was speaking in the house the other day on the same subject he said, as reported at page 908 of Hansard of February 25:
Hon. members have been talking about conscription, about no conscription and the like. That is not the issue in this plebiscite.
If that is not the issue in this plebiscite, in view of the Prime Minister's statement last fall that he would not bring in conscription for overseas service until he had consulted the people, I would ask this question: After this-plebiscite is disposed of, when the government decides to bring in conscription for overseas service, are we to have another plebiscite? Is the Prime Minister then to go to the country on that issue? I believe that is a fair question based upon these two statements of the Prime Minister which I find confusing, with the plebiscite bill in its present form and the question framed as it appears in the bill. I think the minister or the Prime Minister should answer that question while we are in committee, and answer it definitely so that the people will understand.	_	_
Another reason for my confusion is the statement that was made by the Prime Minister, in that same speech, on February 25, as reported at page 914 of Hansard:
We are simply asking to be given freedom to make an untrammeled decision and to come to parliament with that decision. Let my hon. friends beep that in mind, that before any measure can be passed in this parliament, mo matter what it relates to, conscription or anything else, it has to get the support of a majority of the House of Commons and the ministry has to consider very carefully every aspect of the question which will bear upon the situation in presenting any measure to parliament.

Thank you. There were one or two minor changes. One to which I would refer, is the matter of leaving the polling stations open. According to the Dominion Elections Act, polling stations are to be open from eight in the morning until six in the evening. I should like to have seen them kept open for the plebiscite from eight in the morning to eight in the evening, so that many thousands of workers in the factories and elsewhere can exercise their right to vote. An amendment was adopted providing that polling stations should be open until seven o'clock in the evening, which is a step in the right direction.
We have spent far too long on this matter of the plebiscite. However, now that this administration and this parliament have decided to go ahead with it, I hope it will be proceeded with speedily and the matter disposed of without delay. The people of Canada are looking askance at what is happening here, particularly at the time which is being spent. They must feel pretty much like soldiers who have been watching the enemy arm, seeing him approach, and about to attack. Then they are told by some brass-hat to go and polish their shoes. I hope we shall get through rapidly with this bill and have the plebiscite over and done with.

speechtext:
Supplementing the remarks of the hon. member for Yorkton, may I ask the minister whether there is any good reason why the time for polling could not be extended to a little later in the evening. It seems to me that many of these sections were drawn by those who do not fully understand. what the working man has to contend with as regards his hours of leisure. Do hon. members realize that many working people have difficulty) because of the limited number of hours that stores and offices are open, in finding time to attend to their outside business

affairs? I think this is one place where we might well make a concession to the wageearning section of our population, by extending a little the time for voting. In some sections where, perhaps, in a general election the results of the polling are of great importance, there may be some reason for restricting the number of hours, but with all possible emphasis I urge the government to reconsider the period for voting, particularly with a view to its further extension in the evening. I should like to see it so arranged that our working men will not have to line up at the booths during the last part of the day in order to vote. These are some of the busiest people in the country and they should be given proper consideration. I make that suggestion in a friendly and constructive spirit.

speechtext: I am not so sure that is a complete answer to the problem. If I recollect -it is only an offhand recollection-a man working in a factory must make application to his employer to get time off. Arrangements must be made on that basis, and my suggestion would avoid the difficulties which might arise between employer and employee with respect to that request. I cannot see what great damage would result from keeping the polls open another hour, because, after all, some of these workers, particularly in war works, and in places far distant from their homes, have much difficulty in taking the two hours off. Most hon. members realize that. If the workers are a long piece away they must get transportation, and it is much easier for them to vote at the latter part of the day either after supper or when they are coming home. Moreover, it would be more convenient for them. I wish the minister would consider that point. I may be entirely wrong in my contention, 'but I am quite honest in urging it.

I am sorry that the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), the prospective Minister of Agriculture when the Conservatives get into office, forgot about the farming population. Perhaps, when he becomes minister, he will forget the farmers just as much then as he does to-day, but that will only be in keeping with the practice of the present Minister of Agriculture. I rise to protest, as I protested as far back as 1938, against the discrimination that is being carried out in certain provinces-in four of them- against a particular class of citizens who find themselves in very unfortunate circumstances. I refer to section 10 (k) of the regulations covering ordinary voters:
in any province, every person who is^ an inmate of an institution which is maintained by any government or municipality for the housing .a.nd maintenance of the poor, if such person is by the law of that province disqualified from voting at an election of a member of the legislative assembly of that province, and did not serve in the military, naval or air forces of Canada in the war of 1914-1918 or in the war that began in September, 1939.
I am very sorry that this is in effect in the -provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Ontario and British Columbia. Those -hon. members who were on the elections and franchise committee when we revised the -present election act in 1936, 1937 and 1938 will remember that we had a heated discussion on that problem, and in 1939 I brought in an amendment to the elections act which was defeated. We are living in a democratic country, at least under the forms of democracy, and I regret that the people of those provinces, and this parliament, have not seen fit to change those regulations so that we might have the benefits of democracy extended to people who are in our poor institutions. As I have pointed out on- -other occasions, the old age pensioners are demanding pensions because they have been legally ro-b-bed during their years of productive activity, and I believe that if we investigated the cases of a number of those who are in the institutions to which I have referred, we should find exactly
the same position existing. To-day I am asking again, -before this -bill proceeds m-uch further, that parliament take into consideration the plight of those who are in these institutions and give them the right to vote. There is no reason why that right should be denied them. These regulations are manmade, and surely we who are boasting of and fighting for democracy should put enough of our democratic speeches into practice and give these people the right to vote on this and other questions hereafter.

As a member of the special committee I quite agree with the hon. member for Yorkton -that it was never the intention o-f the committee that the ballot papers should be numbered. It is true that in section 15 of the regulations it is provided that the plebiscite officers shall cause the ballot papers to be used at the plebiscite to be printed on both sides, consecutively numbered, perforated and bound, and so on. But if you will look at subsection 2 of section 15 you will find it stated that such ballot papers shall be according to form number 15 and shall *bear the question to be submitted at the plebiscite in the form set out in the said proclamation. Turning to form 15, there is no numbering on the ballot, -but there is on the form a replica of the back of the -ballot- this is on page 76 of the regulations-and- the stub and counterfoil are properly numbered. But the ballot is not numbered and it was never the intention of the committee to have it numbered. N-or was it by any oversight that section 15 of the regulations was passed by the committee, because the voter is protected by the form of ballot as shown in form 15.
The minister, who was chairman of the committee, has made a general statement. He gave us a memorandum of the method of taking the votes of service voters, and under the terms of that memorandum an officer is designated to take the votes of the members of each unit. It is -provided that a ballot paper shall be handed to the voter in tire same form as that used in Canada, in an inner envelope, and he will go to a compartment and mark his ballot and so on. There is no provision whereby the returning officer, or the commissioned officer as the case may be, will initial the counterfoil on the ballot or that the counterfoil will be removed before the ballot is put in the envelope. I expect regulations will be passed to cover that, but this does not -cover it.

speechtext: The leader of the opposition urged the necessity of having those who vote on this plebiscite produce their national registration certificate. The minister has taken the stand, and the committee agreed with the view, that to do so might deprive some people of their vote. As an alternative I suggest to the minister that as to those voters whose right to vote depends upon their being vouched for, in order to guard against the possibility of wrongdoing, the production by such persons of their national registration certificate be made a condition precedent. In that way any suggestion of the possibility of a racket being perpetrated would be entirely obviated. I can see no reason why those whose names are not on the voters' list should not be required to produce their registration certificate as an additional safeguard to those set out in section 7 of the bill.

The other day the minister who is piloting this legislation said that he was open-minded-something everyone knows; we appreciate him for it-and that this bill is not like the laws of the Medes and Persians.

Mr. Chairman, on January 24, a journalist came to me requesting an interview with respect to the plebiscite. I told him that it was impossible to give any definite opinion until the wording was made known, and that I was opposed to any high-pressure or uncalled-for publicity. I said that I favoured free public comprehension and expression, and that I expected the plebiscite would not be after the pattern of Hitler's plebiscite in Austria. I said that the defence of Canada should be completed and assured before our men were conscripted for overseas.
On February 22, the day after the last black-out in the province of Quebec, Miss M. V. Cummings, secretary of the civil protection committee of Quebec city, was interviewed by the press. The [DOT] following is a report:
Throughout the province, Miss Cummings said, especially in the northern Quebec area of Lake St. John and the lower St. Lawrence district, officials reported that everything had run off smoothly. Mies Cummings added that "it is particularly gratifying to see that the most vulnerable points of the province have had such a marked success."
Speaking with respect to the victory loan on Friday, February 20, Premier Godbout of Quebec is reported in La Presse to have said that the province of Quebec is in imminent peril.
One of the most interesting dailies published on this continent is undoubtedly the New York Times. On the front page of the magazine section of the issue of yesterday, March 1, I read this:
But among many prominent officials a number of illusions still exist. They are dangerous illusions, almost as dangerous as those mentioned above, and nowhere are they more evident than in Washington.
The first of these illusions is that since we are the richest and potentially the strongest people in the world we cannot lose the war.

Plebiscite Act
This, of course, is said of the United States.
The second is that we can win the war without using our very best men in government, regardless of party.
The third is that we can win the war without scrapping a number of high military officers and naval commanders who are still thinking in terms of classic defence rather than of modern offence.
The fourth is that the nation will fight its best on a diet of optimistic news and that it is necessary for our government, in order to confuse its enemies, to confuse its own people and its friends.
The fifth is that we can beat the axis on the forty-hour week.
Nothing is more fallacious in time of war than the illusion that money is power. We may be able to solve most of our difficulties with it in peace time, but one cannot stop a tank with a hundred-thousand dollar bill. Even the official dollars-and-oents war production figures dispel this illusion.
The article is headed, "Are We Awake?" and was written by James B. Reston.
On the first page of the editorial section in the same issue there is a map of Asia and the Pacific ocean. Below the map twelve strategic places in the Japanese drive are mentioned. They are as follows:
1.	Thailand submits to the Japanese, December 8.
2.	After siege Hong Kong surrenders, December 25.
3.	British-controlled Sarawak falls, January 1.	_	>
4.	Japanese troops march into Manila, January 2.
5.	Celebes invaded by the Japanese, January 12.
6.	New Britain attacked by Japanese, January 23.
7.	Conquest of Malaya is completed, January 31.
8.	Japanese occupy Amboina naval base, February 7.
9.	Sumatra, flanking Java, invaded, February 14.
10.	Fortress of Singapore surrenders, February 15.
11.	Japanese open struggle for Bali, February 20.
12.	Rangoon is menaced by Japanese, February 27.
On the front page of the issue of Le Soleil of Quebec for February 26 there is a picture of Mr. Dies, the well-known United States congressman, who has discovered Japanese maps showing an invasion plan of the United States through Alaska and northwestern Canada. He states as a fact that those maps were found in the possession of a Japanese spy in the United States. Mr. Dies is photographed with those maps in his hand.
I do not wish to say anything of a secret nature. I wish merely to refresh the memories of hon. members by using clippings which, with few exceptions, have appeared in our own newspapers.
This I have taken from the Ottawa Citizen of February 24:
Canada within range of bombers from Norway. Young Belgian artillery officer declares nazi four-motored machines could make trip easily.
The Ottawa Journal of December 10 contained a dispatch to the effect that Canada was only twelve hours from German air bases. These are the words appearing in the article: Air Commodore Albert de Niverville addressing a luncheon here to-day-
This was in Montreal.
-said Canada was about twelve hours from German air bases. While Halifax is half a day from Brest, Bordeaux and German air bases, our Pacific coast itself must face a new danger resulting from Japan's entry into the conflict.
Several hon. members have mentioned the worry which exists to-day in Australia because of the Japanese coming closer and closer. But that is not all. I hold in my hand a Canadian Press dispatch dated at Wellington, New Zealand, January 25:
British-United. States reply heartens Antipodes.
Prime Minister Peter Fraser said to-day that New Zealand had received a heartening response to pleas to the United States and Britain for aid in the Pacific war. This was the first official disclosure that New Zealand had joined Australia in such appeals.
On June 18 of last year-and I mentioned this fact the other day in the house-at a meeting here in Ottawa the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) said that the need for men was immediate and urgent. He was referring to men for overseas. He asked for volunteers on two grounds, first that Canada could do no less than the British people who stood so bravely on the front line and, second, that men had been pledged to Great Britain. When I asked him for supplementary information, as always he was vague.
During last summer I took the trouble to make a scrap book of news items. I did this for a little over two months, from the end of June to the beginning of September, during which time many important events occurred. One of them was the quick about-turn of Russia. At that time, because of a statement by the Minister of National Defence which appeared in the press, it was stated that the number of men required overseas from Canada was approximately 100,000. According to the papers of February 11 there has been a big jump. I have here the headlines of an article which was published in our contemporaries here in Ottawa. The Minister of National Defence may have made some arrangement with Sir John Dill while he was here or with
Plebiscite Act

Mr. Churchill, because this article states, "Ralston says forces require 193,000 men during present year." That is twice as many as were contemplated during last summer.
There are some people who may be termed armchair strategists because they contend that Canada is menaced. There is a gentleman familiar to all members of parliament who are war veterans. I refer to Mr. Walker, the head of the legion. The Montreal Gazette of February 27 had this to say:
Coasts of Canada fronting danger.
Head of legion, Alex Walker, compares situation to Australia.
Denies scare mongering.
Tragedy facing antipodes real for this dominion unless it prepares itself.
We have been told that submarines have been off the coast of Nova Scotia, and we know that Jap submarines have shelled the coast of California. There is one thing that I cannot understand. If England, which is smaller than a handkerchief on the map when compared with Canada, considers that 4,000,000 men are not enough for her defence, who will say that half a million men would be too many for the defence of Canada? Many times I had occasion to discuss this matter with my very dear and lamented friend, the former Minister of Justice, Mr. Lapointe. One time when he was away one of the acting ministers decided to send men of the mounted police overseas. More than that, applicants for positions in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police had to consent to serving overseas before they were accepted in the force. When I brought Mr. Lapointe's attention to the matter he wrote me the following letter which has been made public and which is on record:
I have your letter of the 3rd August enclosing copy of a page of Hansard and of a communication addressed by you on July 31 to Mr. S. T. Wood, Commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
I have given consideration to your representations regarding certain questions appearing on the form of enlistment in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and concerning the applicants' consent to serve overseas. As you are aware, the question has been settled in the way you wished, and consent to serve overseas is no longer required of applieants for enlistment in the R.C.M.P.
Believe me, dear Mr. Pouliot,
Yours sincerely,
Ernest Lapointe.
That letter was marked "personal", as were all his letters. When I saw Mr. Lapointe about it I told him that that must have been a clerical error, ahd he gave me permission to publish the letter.
Le Canada, is a strong government paper, and a brilliant one too. It is published in Montreal, and I should like to quote an 
editorial which appeared in the issue of February 23, as follows:
The out-and-out advocates of conscription for overseas service should awaken to reality and understand that it would 'be unwise to deprive ourselves of our defenders at the very moment when we are more exposed to attack than ever before. So long as Canada could be considered secure from any attempt at invasion, it was natural that we should contribute to strengthen the United Kingdom, our strongest bulwark against the undertakings of Germany. But it is no longer so. The western part of our country is to-day an area of war. Further striking successes by the Japanese would place us in still graver peril. It must therefore be expected that the government wishes to guard against this danger and will inform members of parliament of the measures it has taken. The secrecy of the proceedings will prevent any advantage accruing to the enemy. On the other hand, * our representatives will know exactly what is being done and will be able, if necessary, to advise the government regarding the nature of our defence preparations.
In the New York Times of March 1 there is a dispatch from Mr. P. J. Philip of Ottawa, dated February 28. This is quite interesting, and it reads as follows:
Coast peril shifts policy in Canada.
Idea that war must be won in Europe is shelved-Pacific strategy role forecast.
Japanese transfer plan.
Board set up to move British Columbia's aliens.
This progress is only on paper. When I first read it I was surprised to see that the government still intended to proceed with the bill. "Joint defence is relevant." Surely my chief, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), remembers what was said by the member for Temiscouata at one of the last sittings of the session that ended in August, 1940. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Fulford) and I were the first to speak about the need for signing a war treaty with the United States, but at that time we were told that it was not an opportune time to mention matters like that. Not long afterward the Prime Minister had an interview with the President of the United States, and matters were arranged for mutual defence. Canada to aid U.S.
Fight any invader on Pacific coasts.
Trainees would go.

Opposition leader poses case of attack on Seattle or Alaska.

I have never been fearful; fear is a feeling that I ignore completely; it is unknown to me. But I am much worried and concerned about the future of this country so long as we forget that this Canada of ours is on mother earth rather than on the planet Mars. Some people seem to be just as indifferent to the fate of this country as though Canada were on the planet Mars. We are surrounded by fearful enemies and we need some protection in this country. Hawaii's defences held inadequate.
Situation not improved since December 7, but more forces are declared required.
It cannot happen again.
Pacific war seen reaching stage where foe might move on islands.

speechtext:
There is always an honest George in Ontario. George Drew was chosen as counsel for the leader of the opposition in the Hong Kong probe, and speaking of that probe the Montreal Gazette says:
There remains the inescapable feeling that secrecy must always beget the feeling that this inquiry was a "government affair". No better means could be found of dissipating this faint distrust than the appointment of Colonel Drew as opposition counsel. Not only was he the initiator, one might even say the source, of the opposition's stand on this issue, but he is of all Canadians now in civil life, one of the best qualified to judge a military question.
I come now to a good Liberal paper, Le Soleil of Quebec. In its editorial of February 23 it complains of the fact that the probe will not be public and goes on to say that it does not see the usefulness of such a procedure unless the investigation is to be based on new
facts as well as on charges and admissions heard in the House of Commons. Le Soleil adds that it is necessary to have a declaration from the government on the matter and asks:
Is it left to the discretion of the tribunal to limit the scope of the inquiry and information promised to parliament and the nation?
I come now to a very fanatical paper, the Ottawa Journal. I shall read only the first paragraph of two articles, one on George Drew and one on my humble self, and members will see how blind are these nasty Tories. I quote first from the Ottawa Journal of Thursday, January 22, 1942, from an editorial entitled "The Rights of a Critic," which says in part.
Col. George Drew, Conservative leader in Ontario, states a truism when he reasserts his right to criticize government activities even in war. It is necessary, however, to maintain this unquestioned democratic right against some who feel, quite honestly, that even well-founded and constructive criticism is "subversive" and to be deplored.
There would be nothing wrong with that. But here is the first paragraph of an article dedicated to the Liberal member for Temis-couata, who had asked for the resignation of the Minister of National Defence, who pTobably leases some floor space in the Ottawa Journal's building. This article in the Journal's issue of February 20, headed, "Sort of thing that hurts parliament," reads in part:
On the principle that one cannot argue from the particular to the general it would be wrong to condemn parliament for the antics of Mr. Jean-Frangois Pouliot. Yet Mr. Pouliot's silly sub-amendment to the speech from the throne, asking the house to condemn the government for "contemplating" conscription, is precisely the sort of thing which leaves many people contemptuous of parliament. What is wrong, it is asked-what is wrong with a democratic institution which, at this time, seems powerless to put a stop to such palpable tomfoolery?
I take great comfort in the thought that in every province, particularly in Ontario, provincial governments are enlarging their lunatic asylums, and I have no doubt that there will be room in one of the new wards for the fellow who wrote that.
The fall of Hong Kong was deeply felt by all. There is one thing that happened there, and that is that our soldiers were sent without equipment and without ammunition. Of course, some responsibility might rest with the Minister of National Defence. But he was not alone. There was a very high officer, there is now, who was inspector-general of the western command, and he is no less than Tory Senator Griesbach. How could our men have left for Hong Kong without the approval of the inspector-general of the army? My fear is that the appointment of George Drew
Plebiscite Act

on the Hong Kong probe is precisely to give a whitewash to Senator Griesbach. I see the leader of the opposition laughing. I would not have expected him to do it because what I say is the truth. He knows I am not afraid to tell the truth, and I say that the man who is responsible must be held guilty for such a thing occurring. It is not the quartermaster-general who should be punished for that. It is the inspector-general of the western command, who is a Tory senator, and he should be fired at once, and moreover, should be court-martialed.
I have another clipping here headed, "Bennett explains fall of Singapore." This was the commander of the Australian imperial force in Malaya, and he blames the fall of Singapore on the lack of water, heavy bombing, and greatly superior numbers. The British had no means of flying from Singapore.

It shows a silk-hatted politician with a book in his hand, and beside him in the jungle handling a machine gun are two Australian soldiers. The cartoon has the politician saying:
No reinforcements yet-but I'm sent to read you this parliamentary debate proving:
