Here is a gentleman from New Brunswick, not Viscount Bennett, but Lord Beaverbrook himself, who is quoted in the New York Herald-Tribune of June 9, 1941, as saying:
Adolf Hitler had "given youth its head" in his plans and preparations, and Britain now found itself confronted "with a mentality which makes rings around many of our old ideas", he said.
Mr. Malcolm MacDonald, High Commissioner for Great Britain in Canada, made an appeal in Toronto the other day to send Canadians overseas. Here is what this gentleman said when he set foot on Canadian shores, according to a dispatch by Mr. John Marshall, a very able journalist and president of the press gallery. This article appeared in the Windsor Daily Star of April 4, 1941. Speaking of the British people, for whom I have a deep admiration because I know them well-the

only ones who do not deserve admiration are the British politicians with the exception of Mr. Churchill-Mr. MacDonald said:	,
Even if they were fighting alone, they couldn't be beaten. But, they are not alone.
Et cetera. And he said that our help was superfluous. But I have something still better in my hand, and it is-again-that Tory paper, the Ottawa Journal. Some interesting news is contained in its five o'clock edition, July 3, 1940:
Want Canadians to halt nazis if they land.
Dominion troops have "more novel conception of warfare".
London. July 3-(CP)-Lord Mottistone, who as "Jack" Seely commanded the Canadian cavalry in the first great war, suggested in the House of Lords to-day that Canadian troops should be chosen to engage the enemy if he lands in Britain because of their "more novel conception of warfare".
He recommended the Canuck soldiers not because he served with them in the last war for 3J years "and so knew their value", but because amongst these Canadian divisions-and this also applies to other divisions overseas where there are wider spaces-there are people with more novel conceptions of warfare.
Lord Mottistone said he had made the suggestion to a Canadian officer with a distinguished record, who had replied "that just suits me".
What did Sir Stafford Cripps, the present Lord Privy Seal, say the other day? Coming from Russia, he told us many things which are very interesting; he endorsed our victory loan, and he complained that a full effort was not being made at the present time in Great Britain. Mr. Eden, and also many labour leaders, spoke along the same line.
Some years ago, in this honourable house, sitting in committee of the whole, I objected strongly to red tape. Here is what the member for Temiseouata said about red tape, Hansard, February 22, 1937, page 1124:
Red tape must disappear from the Department of National Defence. I am in favour of a good army to defend our country, but I want no red tape and I want no other people than good Canadians to defend our own country.
And then:
I blame the bureaucracy that has been established there

In the Department of National Defence.
-a long time. . . . There are some in the department who were hiding themselves when the others were fighting-
In the last war.
-and now they are the bosses and try to run the whole show. Enough of that; it must stop. Representatives of the people must bring them to their senses.
Previously I had said, at page 1120:
Some people are fond of brass hats and so on; I do not care for them. . . .

Plebiscite Act
Here is the definition which the member for Temiscouata gave at that time, as quoted in the Windsor Star:
These people in the Department of National Defence cannot learn -warfare. They must be trying out their penmanship all the time. Everybody in that department, from the chief of staff to the last appointed stenographer, must also be a typist. We hear a lot about that- most foolish; most stupid-and it continues like that.
This we call red tape. What is red tape? Red tape consists of a lot of formalities carried out just to show the importance of the one who performs them. Red tape is useless, but it is made use of for a purpose. It is carried out to show that the man who executes the formalities is the only man who could do this well. In the civil service my experience , ha.s been that the simplest things, the easiest to understand, are made the most difficult in order to show the ability and the wonderful genius of an ass. Hon. members laugh, but that is the case. Let us take the fellow who is stupid, and who cannot do anything well. He says, "I will make myself important." Then he assumes a solemn air, and attempts to convince his minister that he is the only being on earth who can do a certain thing. Sometimes he is believed; sometimes the officials do not see the ears of the ass. There is a lot of that, but I shall not insist upon it.
This is enough for the moment. I want to put this on record as a preface to what I am going to say and to move afterwards.

I am astounded that the most simple things, things that are based on common sense, are so hard to put into the heads of those in power. I cannot understand it. The more simple a thing is, the more difficult it is to have it accepted.
It is said that we shall have a plebiscite to decide whether we shall send men overseas by conscription, or whether we shall not. We are to decide whether or not the government is to be relieved from a promise made in the past. Why were those promises made? They were made on account of the deep patriotic feeling of the population of Canada, who wanted some protection provided by the Department of National Defence. At the present time what we have is very small, if it exists at all.
We are going on with the plebiscite; we are asking the people if they are willing to relieve the government from what is called the prosecution of the war. What reason does the government give for being relieved of its commitment given during the past year? None at all. Not a single reason has been given by any minister or any hon. member to justify the plebiscite. So much is that so that the Prime Minister said, "I do not know if I need it now, but I may need it later. But, trust me." I trust the Prime Minister; I have supported him for a great many years. Mr. Chairman, I have risen several times to speak for a few minutes, and I shall detain the committee for only three or four minutes. There is a rule in the house that in committee an hon. member may speak as often as he wishes. He may speak in English and in French, or both, if he chooses.
I have no objection to the minister now making headway with his bill clause by clause, but I should like to point out three or four facts-because facts are facts. I am opposed to the principle of "follow your leader" and "your leader is your policy" on an important measure like this. Every day the bill is before the house the government shift their position with respect to the principle and policy of this bill. They began by telling the country, before parliament met, that owing to the scarcity of man-power the government were going to take some steps at the coming session of parliament, and announced a plebiscite. The reason for it and the cause and effect of the vote have been changed.
The government did announce a policy in the speech from the throne. Now they are
Plebiscite Act

shifting their position. They shifted it in the house, and they shifted it again in the committee the other day and now in this committee, and in all the debates we have had so far. It was said there was great difficulty in getting sufficient man-power and the government were going to lay down a new policy. Then they come along before the house met and propose a plebiscite or a referendum. This has never been done before except that one was held in 1898 in the days of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. In that referendum there were 200 local votes off it taken all over Ontario and Manitoba. The Prime Minister made a speech last Wednesday of a different nature. What is the cause and effect of this plebiscite bill, the first we have ever had in Canada, now under the title of the Dominion Plebiscite Act, 1942? The cause is the failure to get man-power or to do anything for a total war. Last Wednesday the Prime Minister said, as reported at page 826 of Hansard:
Hon. members have been talking about conscription, about no conscription and the like. That is not the issue in this plebiscite. This is the issue: Is the government of Canada, in time of war, to have freedom to take whatever action it thinks most advisable with respect to the furtherance of Canada's war effort?
If that is the question, then what is the plebiscite for and why is it at all necessary? Have the government of Canada no courage to act and govern, and do their duty when the enemy is at our very gates? The Japs have submarines that can cross the Pacific without refuelling. As the Prime Minister of Great Britain told the House of Commons the other day, we shall have to expect the enemy who now have captured the command of the sea in the Pacific and will appear on many islands and shores of many countries in the Pacific, and in many other places. If you had a million men, he said, you would not be able to stop them because they move from one island and place to another like a circus from place to place. If the enemy appear in time in the inlets and harbours of British Columbia, will the commanding officer there have to wire Ottawa and say that the enemy is there and will he have to hold a plebiscite before firing a gun, or before sending up an aeroplane?
That is what they would have had to do under the Laurier naval bill in 1909. The same principle applies or may apply with this plebiscite bill to-day. If the enemy in 1909 had approached on the ocean, before the then Canadian navy could have fired off a pin-wheel, a fire-cracker or a sky-rocket, they would have had to have an order in council passed here in Ottawa first, under the naval bill of 1909. That was the principle of the navy bill. Are
[Mr. Church.)
we going to have the same principle in this bill? The people of the country are awake to what is going on. They know more than we do about this plebiscite. They look upon it as being absolutely unnecessary. They consider that with the enemy at our doors, it is no time for it or for playing so at war. The situation is too grave for such by-play.
What will happen when the vote is taken? The ballot in this bill has black all round it and we may have a black-out here with Hitler and Japan arriving first before we can vote yes or no. The enemy may arrive before we can go into the polling booth and mark yes or no. The ballot reads:
Are you in favour of releasing the government from any obligation arising out of any past commitments restricting the methods of raising men for military service?
I would strike out all the words after the word "government" and have the ballot read, "Are you in favour of releasing the government?" It is the government that is asking for a release and that is the question to submit, if any. Some pledges were given, but we do not know to whom they were given and conscription was not an issue. I tell you what will happen. Instead of government of the people, by the people and for the people, what have we in this country to-day? We have government by order in council-twenty to twenty-five thousand of them- government by plebiscite and, in addition, government by dollar-a-year men. Is it any wonder that the people are losing confidence in this parliament? Is it any wonder that the electors are asking if there is any parliamentary government or any semblance of it left in this country, or if we are trying to imitate the methods of a mock parliament by this bill? That is what I think we are trying to do, and just playing at war.
When the vote is counted, what will happen? This is going to tie up our war effort for three months; it is going to throttle our effort in the most critical months of the year, April, May and June. We may not know to whom this country belongs by June the way things are going on with the Japs in the Pacific. I tell you what will happen to your vote. The minute the ballots are counted, they will simply be taken to the archives for decent burial of it all in that big new building, where it will be a case of "earth to earth, ashes to ashes and dust to dust" for this plebiscite; in the sure, certain hope, so far as this plebiscite on conscription is concerned, it will never be mentioned by the government again. That will be the end of it.
The Prime Minister made a magnificent speech the other day. I have never heard such a magnificent speech since the old days

Plebiscite Act
when he was a student going to university and when the temperance orators of the world used to speak each week-end in the city of Toronto. We heard a lot of oratory in those days in Massey hall, which was a new building then. The oratory in Massey hall was no better than what we heard here the other day. If it was simply a matter of taking a vote on who was to sign the pledge, it would be a different matter. But it is more than that. The voters know more than we do. They are not going to be humbugged or fooled or consent to be blindfolded by members of parliament or anybody else. A lot of them will not vote. A lot of ballots will be spoiled. No one understands it. Many of them think it is an insult to the electors of this country that this house should sit here day after day discussing academic matters and that kind of thing when the enemy in the Pacific have command of the sea, and when they may get it in the Atlantic as well.
If it were not for Russia, I do not know where we would be. The greatest friends the allies have had are General January and General February. If it had not been for General January and General February in the war between Germany and Russia, we would not know where the British empire would be. General January and General February, this year also are the best friends that British Columbia ever had. They saved the coast province after Pearl Harbour. They have given them a chance in British Columbia to get started and try to arm.
I protest against this bill, and if I can get a seconder I shall move the six months' hoist on the third reading. I believe the rank and file of the members of this house should have an opportunity of placing the blame where it belongs, on the government.
Hon. members opposite have brought in this bill just as a smoke-screen to cover up the mistakes made in the Pacific, Singapore, Hong Kong and other places. We had the Prime Minister rising the other night and wanting to have a dozen moTe Hong Kongs without consulting the military authorities in the sending of troops to adjacent territory, to Seattle, the Aleutian islands and other places where there are no military objectives. This was to be done over the heads of the military authorities by politicians, against the strategy and priorities set out by the Prime Minister of Great Britain. I protest against this.
My constituents can vote the way they want to. They know better than I how to vote. We had two governments in my riding in 1934. We had the whole dominion cabinet down there in 1934 in the by-election and we had the cabinet of the province of Ontario
also. They all appeared there and I was glad to see them. The people of Toronto know how to vote without my telling them. I believe I know how they will vote. They will throw the ballot back in the faces of the government and say, "You have been elected to run the war, not us; go and carry on the work; as long as you are the government of the day, the responsibility is on your shoulders to see to it that we have a magnificent new war effort and a new war management."

Mr. Chairman, I was one of the members of the special committee to which this bill was referred. The members of that committee gave careful consideration to each section of the bill, and while they did not all see eye to eye in every particular, they were all agreed on this, that the bill as it came before the committee was too wide in its scope. I am glad to say they all agreed on that; and as a consequence the bill that comes before this committee to-day varies in its most essential provision from the bill as originally drafted and presented to the house. As originally drafted, the bill contained a principle-the Speaker may not agree with me, but I say that it was a principle-that is not to be found in the bill as it is now before this committee. The underlying principle of the bill as first presented to the house was that the government could by proclamation order the taking of a plebiscite at any time it saw fit. That provision was contained in section 3, subsection 1 of the bill as drafted, which read as follows:
The governor in council may by proclamation order the taking of a plebiscite under the provisions of this act.
That was a most dangerous provision. If it had become law it would have made a radical change in the constitution of this country. It would have led the way to government by plebiscite-something which we should endeavour to avoid in Canada. Under our constitution-I may not be speaking accurately but this is as I understand it- the decision of the people on any matter of public policy is given and given only through their elected representatives. Within its legislative jurisdiction the power of parliament is supreme. If the government wants to change its policy or adopt a new policy, it must submit it to parliament for its approval, and if approval is not given, the government must dismiss parliament and appeal to the electors.
Our system of parliamentary government does not provide for any other procedure. It does not provide for procedure by plebiscite.

Plebiscite Act
The two courses open to a government if it wants to change its policy are (1) to have parliament approve the change, or (2) to dissolve parliament and have a new parliament deal with the matter after an election has been held.
To have an important change made in our constitution by the passing of this bill as originally drafted and presented to the house would have been most undesirable and was to be avoided at all costs. It was, I think, with that thought in mind that the members of the special committee limited the provisions of the bill.
The reason why the government introduces this bill is to ask the voters of this country to release it from a promise which it made. That promise was, that there would be no conscription of our man-power for service overseas. The bill as it has been amended by the special committee limits or circumscribes the legislation to that particular question.
I do not think this legislation should be regarded as a precedent, or as changing in any way our constitution. It should be regarded- and I think the special committee looked at it in that light

as extraordinary legislation arising under special conditions brought about in war time. If it is so regarded, I do not believe that, speaking from a constitutional point of view, it can do any harm. But that is the way it should be looked at, and some emphasis should be put upon that phase of the matter by the members of the government who are interested in the bill.
I was impressed with the point made this afternoon by the leader of the opposition, that the regulations impose certain penalties, but that those regulations do not come before parliament but are made by order in council. It seems to me that we are neglecting our duties as members of the House of Commons in not paying more attention to that particular matter.
I would refer also briefly to the suggestion of the hon. member for Lake Centre this afternoon, that any person whose name was omitted from the voters' list, and wanted it added thereto should, in addition to making the affidavits for which the regulations provide, produce his registration certificate. That is a very wise proposal; it would provide an effective safeguard.

The first was in connection with the form of ballot to be used on the plebiscite, which is set out under section 3. When this section was before the committee I suggested that another form of ballot be used, whereby the question would be set out at the top of the ballot, and there would follow one, two or three lines of instructions to the voter as to how to mark his ballot; then there would be a space for the word "yes" and underneath that a space for the word "no." I know I am of small stature, Mr. Chairman, but some time I may fill the shoes of a Minister of Agriculture, and then perhaps I can be seen and heard. The hon. member for Caribou has called attention to the wording of the ballot paper and suggested that when people vote they will read what is at the top of the ballot. I am more concerned as to what the people will read about in respect to what they are voting for. I am more confused about that than I am about the form of the ballot. The question to be asked of the voters is this:
Are you in favour of releasing the government from any obligation arising out of any past commitments restricting the methods of raising men for military service?
I have tried to think my way through that, and I can think of only two methods of raising men: One is by conscription and the other is by voluntary enlistment. There may be some regulations governing methods. The government may be confused over whether they should send a postcard when a man is to be called up for military service or whether they should send an officer along to tell him lie is required. I would ask the minister what methods of raising men for military service are used now, and what commitments have been made that restrict the government to any particular methods of raising men. I do not believe that the government are restricted in their methods of raising men. Where they are restricted is as to where to send the men after they are raised. But that does not appear on the ballot, and I think people are going to be confused as to what they are voting for when they read the question.
While on the question of the ballot, I appreciate the minister's suggestion that we let the ballot stand until he can reconsider its form. But if he is going to reconsider the ballot at all, there are a few other matters he should consider, and first is the thing I have already mentioned, the question to be asked. but I will submit it for consideration, and if this is the time to vote on it, the minister may accept it and embody it in the ballot for our consideration when he comes back. I move that the following words be added to the question appearing on the ballot paper: "in any theatre of war." The question then will read:
Are you in favour of releasing the government from any obligation arising out of any past commitments restricting the methods of raising men for military service in any theatre of war.
Then the people will know what they are voting upon. I think it is only fair to say that the whole country believes that they are going to vote on whether or not there shall be conscription of men for service. But that is not what the ballot states.
There is another thing about this ballot. I have received a good many letters recently in connection with the plebiscite, and the general contention of the people who have inquired of me is that they are not going to vote for the conscription of men for overseas service if they are not privileged to vote on the conscription of finance. I think that is a reasonable attitude to take because, after all, the man who is conscripted to face shot and shell and who gives his life for his country is giving all he has. Surely there should be some mobilization and conscription of other things too. The government desires to be released from its commitments. I would suggest that another question be added to the ballot paper, and I would suggest that it read this way. I move this as an amendment:

speechtext: The hon. member for Qu'Appelle has, I think, put his finger right on the fallacy of this question. In the mobilization act, in the admissions made by the Prime Minister in this house within a few days, the principle of compulsion is admitted. This government has power to raise men by any method, and it is raising them by all the methods which are now available-the voluntary system and the compulsory system. The only distinction is as to the disposition of the men raised by the government. In the one case, the men raised by compulsion may not be sent beyond the territorial limits of Canada, while men raised by voluntary methods may. So the question which is proposed to be put in this ballot is an untruthful one; it does not bear the essence of truth. There is not any restriction to-day on the method of raising men; it is the matter of the disposal of the men once they are raised; there is the fallacy of the whole thing. I put it to the Prime Minister, is there any restriction of the method of raising men in this country to-day? None whatever. The government can do anything it likes under the War Measures Act.

Last year I saw a questionnaire which was put to trainees, and they were chased "right up into the clearing"; if they were not prepared to volunteer for overseas service, why? Men are

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
I am coming back to what was said in the course of the debate on the address. Great emphasis was laid on the importance of having the question that was to be asked before the house when we were discussing the matter, and in speaking on the address I used the following language, as reported in Hansard at page 51:
I shall not go into detail regarding the procedure to be followed in holding the proposed plebiscite. The question which the government proposes to submit to the people is the simple and straightforward question:
Are you in favour of releasing the government from any obligation arising out of any past commitments restricting the methods of raising men for military service?
That was informing the house at the earliest possible moment of what the question would be. At a later stage in the debate, and in the debate on this present bill, some question was raised as to the exact wording of the
question, and I had occasion then to refer the house or the committee to what I had said on the address. This question has been before the house since the house opened, and until to-night the language of it has not been questioned, with respect to any ulterior motive, at least, that may have been in the mind, or as alleged to-night to have been in the mind, of the ministry in the drafting of it. I submit that there is nothing ulterior about the question at all. It is a straightforward question, and inasmuch as the discussion has taken place up to the present in reference to the question in the form in which it is, I hope that hon. members will not suggest the necessity of making any amendments to it.
May I say further that the reason why the question is before us as a part of the bill is largely due to the fact that my hon. friend the leader of the opposition asked that it should be inserted in the bill in the exact words in which it is. If he thought that the question was wrong, or that there was anything ulterior about it, or that there was any duplicity in the wording of it, and so forth, he should not have been the first to suggest that that identical question should be made a part of the bill. It was on my hon. friend's suggestion, that the question as he understood it should be a part of the bill, that I asked that instructions be given to the special committee to see that the question should be so inserted in the bill. I think that ought to be a sufficient reason why at this stage of the debate at any rate the question should not be altered one way or the other.
As to the question, the leader of the opposition now says that the government has the power under the War Measures Act-that it has the power in law and in fact to send men overseas, and that therefore there is no necessity for the question. I have said from the beginning that parliament is all-powerful. As a matter of fact parliament can at the present time pass any enactment it pleases regardless of any commitment that has been made in the past, or any pledge that has been given; but whether parliament would be prepared to do that or not depends a good deal upon what value a man attaches to his word, or what value parliament attaches to its action, or what value a government attaches to its pledge. As to the power, no one has ever denied that parliament has power to do whatever it pleases. With regard to the actual power it possesses to-day to conscript men to send overseas, we have that power under the War Measures Act.
But what was the nature of the pledge that was given, the pledge given on every platform, not by myself alone? I quoted and placed on Hansard od Wednesday last the

Plebiscite Act

strong and emphatic language used by the leader of the Conservative party pledging all his party in exactly the same way as I was pledging mine. It was not as I say in reference to not possessing the power that any pledge was given, but having the power, that the power would not be exercised in one particular; that commitment was made. The pledge admitted the power, if you wish, but the commitment was that that power would not be exercised in one form or particular, namely, raising men for military service overseas by conscription. The commitment was a commitment restricting the methods of raising men for military service. The restriction was as to raising men by conscription for military service overseas.
Now the hon. leader of the opposition seeks to-night to make out that the question as it is worded here is related to the law or to the fact. It is not related to the law or to the fact at all; it is related to a commitment that was made with respect to whatever law there might be or whatever the fact might be. A commitment that no matter whatever power the government had, it would not exercise that power with respect to men to be sent overseas if the method to be employed was to be the method of conscription. In other words, that as far as service overseas was concerned that was to be by voluntary enlistment, not by enlistment under coercion or conscription. That was a commitment. That is the commitment. It is that commitment that the government is asking to be freed from. That commitment does not apply to the use of conscription generally; we have conscription with respect to the raising of men for service in Canada; this parliament itself has enacted a measure which contains the power of the use of compulsion for military service. No exception was taken by the government to that; in fact the government brought forward the measure. The commitment that was made at the time of the general election was not against applying compulsory service for the defence of Canada within Canada; it was only in relation to service overseas. That is why I said the other night that if to-morrow it became necessary to exercise compulsion in the matter of protecting our shores to the extent of our armed forces going out in the Pacific beyond Queen Charlotte island, or to Alaska, or to Labrador or Newfoundland, I would not hesitate one moment in using the War Measures Act to sde that conscription was enforced for that purpose were such a step necessary. That would not be violating the commitment made. The commitment was not made with respect to the protection of our own shores; it was made with respect to sending men

overseas; everyone so understood it, and it was to that extent that the law and the fact was limited and that the government at the present time is limited.
If we attached no importance whatsoever to a solemn pledge given in relation to this particular war, as respects one aspect and one phase of our war effort, then I might join as my hon. friend is prepared to do now, but was not prepared to do at the time he asked the people to return him to parliament; we might say, as he does, discount all that and pay no further attention to it. But we are not prepared so to do; we are going to stand by the pledge we have made until the people themselves release us from it. But we are going to tell the people that we believe it is in their own interest that the government should be released from that pledge or commitment. That is the simple question we are putting before them, the one and only question:
Are you in favour of releasing the government from any obligation arising out of-
Not the law, not the fact, but-
-any past commitments-
[DOT]-and "any past commitments" and "any" covers everything that can be construed as a commitment.
-restricting the methods of raising men for military service.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTE ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY OF PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
-"arising out of any past commitments restricting the methods of raising men for military service." "Any" covers everything, overseas, and all else. What more could any one wish for? That is the whole purpose. So that there can be no doubt whatsoever with respect to any commitment that has been made, whether it relates to any theatre of war or any part of the world, or any aspect of the war service, it covers everything. That is as clear as it possibly can be, and I am saying it as emphatically as I can.
I agree with those who have spoken to-night as to the form of the ballot and who have said that the simpler it can be made the better. I so expressed myself to the minister when I saw what the committee had recommended, but when I heard that the special committee, composed of members of all parties in the house, were unanimously of the view, after having heard the chief electoral officer, that this form of ballot which is now on the order paper was preferable, I said nothing further about it. And for the same reason I thought I would refrain from

Plebiscite Act
saying anything on the matter in the debate to-night. However I think what has been suggested by the hon. member for Yukon, by the hon. member for Carleton, by the leader of the opposition and by several other speakers and what I know the minister himself would prefer would be that there should be but the one simple question, and that at the end of the question there should be a square divided into four with "yes" and "no" above and below each item in the squares nearest the question and two blanks opposite in one or other of which an X could be placed. It would be a very simple ballot, and I would be surprised if the house generally would not agree upon it.
May I say-it may sound a little absurd but I have sometimes thought that if one wanted to get from any group-I am not applying this to this honourable house, but as something to be secured from any group- just the opposite of what might appear to be what is desired, the thing to do would be to suggest the opposite form of question in the first instance, because exception would be bound to be taken to it at the outset. I am as sure as that I am speaking to-night that if the committee had brought in a single question in the form now being proposed we would have had an equal number of speakers asking why we did not put the question into two columns so that there could be no mistake if a person marked his ballot after the "yes" he meant "yes" in regard to that particular question.
I am of the point of view of the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) who said a moment ago that these are terrible times, and I do not think it discloses the truest sense of proportion that we should be spending an entire evening, as we have tonight, listening to one or two hon. members speaking at very great length with the remainder of the time pretty well taken up entirely with a discussion on the wording on a single ballot in respect to which consideration had already been given by a special committee of the house. There are grave issues at stake at the present time, and we may very soon have to consider some of them much more profoundly than we have thus far had occasion to do. I would suggest to hon. members that they try to make all the progress that can be made with the legislation before us, avoiding unnecessarily long speeches and also unnecessary and sometimes trivial objections to what may be before the house.

speechtext:
I agree with the Prime Minister that we are spending far too much time on this plebiscite. There are other and graver issues, we should be dealing with them instead of wrangling over the wording of the plebiscite. But I agree with the amendment of the hon. member for Macleod. The Prime Minister himself is a master of English, and if he reads the question carefully he will find that the words "restricting the methods of raising men for military service" modify the word "commitments," and that the commitments were made in relation to sending men overseas. The adding of the four words "in any theatre of war" would clear the matter up, and make the position abundantly clear. I am asking the Prime Minister and the government to consider the matter over night, because it is now eleven o'clock.
